draft.title: Multi-stage experiments
card: A multi-stage experiment has two or more steps, such as drawing two counters or rolling a die twice. A tree diagram shows each stage as a set of branches, with the probability written on each branch.
To find the probability of one path, multiply along its branches. To find the probability of an outcome that can happen by more than one path, add the path probabilities.
the item is put back, so the second stage has the same probabilities as the first.

the item is kept out, so the total and possibly the favourable count drop by 1 at the second stage. Example: a bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. P(both red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10.
draft.remember: Multiply along a path, add across paths, and check whether the second stage has changed.

a.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(both red)?
a.why: The first draw gives 4/10. With one red gone, the second gives 3/9. So P = 4/10 × 3/9 = 12/90 = 2/15. The option 4/25 comes from 4/10 × 4/10, which wrongly puts the counter back.
a.clue: After the first draw, both the reds and the total change.

b.q: A box has 3 green and 2 yellow balls. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(exactly one green)?
b.why: Two paths work: green then yellow is 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10, and yellow then green is 2/5 × 3/4 = 3/10. Add them: 3/10 + 3/10 = 3/5. The option 12/25 comes from using replacement, where the answer is 2 × 3/5 × 2/5.
b.clue: Find both orders, then add them.
